Sequential AIPE Check for the Coefficient of Variation

Source: R/seq_aipe_cv.R
seq_aipe_cv.Rd

Checks, with the data collected so far, whether enough observations are in hand for a confidence interval for the population coefficient of variation \(\kappa = \sigma / \mu\) (the standard deviation relative to the mean) that is no wider than a chosen width, without assuming a distribution and without a planning value for \(\kappa\). This is the sequential accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) procedure of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018).

Usage

seq_aipe_cv(x, width, conf_level = 0.95)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector: the observations collected so far, at least 4 of them. Missing or infinite values are an error.

width

The target full width of the confidence interval for \(\kappa\) (\(\omega\) in the cited article): the upper limit minus the lower limit, on the scale of the coefficient of variation as a proportion (not a percentage). A single positive number.

conf_level

The confidence level of the interval, a single number strictly between 0 and 1. Default 0.95.

Value

An object of class c("smsd_check", "data.frame") (see smsd_check_methods for its print(), summary(), and tidy() methods) with one row per quantity and columns term and value. The rows are, in order:

lower_limit

the lower confidence limit (NA when the variance estimate is not yet usable or the estimate cannot be computed; see the section below);

cv

the estimated coefficient of variation, as a proportion (NA when the sample mean is zero, negative, or positive only by rounding error);

upper_limit

the upper confidence limit (NA whenever lower_limit is);

xi_squared

the estimated asymptotic variance \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\), at least \(n^{-3}\) (the bound itself when the estimate is not yet usable);

criterion_n

the sample size the stopping rule currently requires (at least current_n + 1 when the variance estimate is not yet usable or the estimate cannot be computed);

current_n

the current sample size.

The object also carries these attributes:

is_satisfied

TRUE when the stopping rule is met, otherwise FALSE; never NA, and always identical to current_n >= criterion_n;

method

the string "coefficient of variation";

current_n, criterion_n

the values in the rows of those names;

conf_level, width

the values supplied;

variance_unusable

TRUE when the raw variance estimate is zero, negative, or not finite (see the section below), otherwise FALSE;

notes

a character vector, empty unless something needs explaining.

Details

The function evaluates the stopping rule once and returns. The user collects the pilot sample (see seq_aipe_cv_pilot), calls seq_aipe_cv(), and, while the rule is not met, adds one or more observations and calls it again. The function prints nothing and keeps no state.

Estimate. The coefficient of variation is estimated by \(k_n = s_n / \bar{X}_n\) (their Equation 11). It is defined for a population with a positive mean, and is most meaningful for ratio scale measurements (times, amounts, counts). Individual observations may be negative, but a sample mean that is zero or negative cannot estimate \(\kappa\); because that can happen by chance in a small early sample, it is reported as "not yet estimable" rather than as an error (see the section below). So is a mean that differs from zero only by rounding error, as the mean of centered or standardized scores does (the coefficient of variation is not meaningful for such scores); the same test is applied by seq_mr_cv.

Stopping rule. Sampling stops at the first \(n\), at or after the pilot size, with $$n \ge \left\lceil \frac{4 z_{\alpha/2}^2}{\omega^2} \left(\hat{\xi}_n^2 + \frac{1}{n}\right) \right\rceil$$ (their Equation 22), where \(\hat{\xi}_n^2\) is the distribution free estimator of the asymptotic variance of \(\sqrt{n}(k_n - \kappa)\) in their Equations 31 and 32, built from the sample mean and variance and unbiased estimates of the third and fourth central moments. The reported interval is \(k_n \pm z_{\alpha/2} \hat{\xi}_n / \sqrt{n}\) (their Equation 33). Whenever the rule is met, the width of that interval is at most width.

Chattopadhyay and Kelley (2016) treat the same estimator under a minimum risk criterion (see seq_mr_cv). The variance in their Equations 9 and 22 agrees with the one used here for normal data and differs otherwise; the 2018 form used here is the distribution free variance.

What the guarantee is. The width guarantee is exact. The coverage guarantee is asymptotic: coverage approaches conf_level as width shrinks (their Theorem 5). At the settings of the article's Table 4 (\(\kappa = 0.2\), width = 0.04, 95%, one observation added at each stage) coverage is close to nominal: 0.936 for normal data and 0.933 for gamma data in 5,000 simulated studies each (the article reports 0.942 and 0.934), with about 240 observations at the end. At targets that are wide relative to \(\kappa\) the final sample is small and coverage falls short. With \(\kappa = 0.5\), coverage was 0.88 for gamma data and 0.79 for lognormal data at width = 0.2 (10,000 studies each, about 52 and 62 observations at the end), and 0.79 and 0.69 at width = 0.4 (6,000 studies each, about 16 observations). The variance estimate was zero or negative in at most 2% of the pilot samples in these conditions, and positive but below \(n^{-3}\), so that the bound was used and the rule met with an interval far narrower than requested, in 12 and 20 of the 6,000 studies at width = 0.4 and in none of 2,000 at width = 0.2; the shortfall comes from the small final sample rather than from the bound. Use seq_aipe_cv_sensitivity to study a planned study before collecting data.

Estimates That Are Not Yet Usable

When the raw variance estimate is zero (exactly, or to within rounding error), negative, or not finite, which is common at small sample sizes for some effect sizes, or when the point estimate cannot be computed (a sample with no variation, where values that agree to ten significant digits count as equal), the check reports the stopping rule as not met, sets attr(out, "variance_unusable") to TRUE, and attaches a note that print() shows; see smsd_check_methods. This is a deliberate departure from the stopping rule as printed in the source articles, under which the lower bound \(n^{-3}\) would stand in for such an estimate and the rule would be met at once with an interval far narrower than requested; a positive estimate, however small, is used as the articles prescribe (the larger of it and \(n^{-3}\)).

References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Chattopadhyay, B., & Kelley, K. (2016). Estimation of the coefficient of variation with minimum risk: A sequential method for minimizing sampling error and study cost. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 51(5), 627–648. doi:10.1080/00273171.2016.1203279

Kelley, K. (2007). Sample size planning for the coefficient of variation from the accuracy in parameter estimation approach. Behavior Research Methods, 39(4), 755–766. doi:10.3758/BF03192966

Maxwell, S. E., Kelley, K., & Rausch, J. R. (2008). Sample size planning for statistical power and accuracy in parameter estimation. Annual Review of Psychology, 59, 537–563. doi:10.1146/annurev.psych.59.103006.093735

See also

seq_aipe_cv_pilot for the pilot size, seq_aipe_cv_sensitivity to simulate the procedure before collecting data, and seq_mr_cv for the minimum risk point estimation counterpart. In DMAR: ss_aipe_cv, the fixed sample size analog for when a planning value of \(\kappa\) is available, ci_cv, and cv.

Other seq_aipe_cv: seq_aipe_cv_pilot(), seq_aipe_sensitivity

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Francis Bilson Darku fbilsond@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# How variable are response times (in milliseconds) on a decision task,
# relative to their mean? The aim is a 95% confidence interval for the
# coefficient of variation that is no wider than 0.15.
set.seed(113)
m <- seq_aipe_cv_pilot(width = 0.15)
response_time <- rgamma(m, shape = 6.25, scale = 80)
out <- seq_aipe_cv(response_time, width = 0.15)
out
#> Sequential check (coefficient of variation)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 27
#>   Criterion n     : 59
#>   Target width    : 0.15
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 0.3024828
#>   cv                : 0.3862728
#>   upper_limit       : 0.4700628
#>   xi_squared        : 0.04934597
#>   criterion_n       : 59
#>   current_n         : 27
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: FALSE

# The rule is not met at the pilot. Add one participant at a time and
# check again, until it is.
while (!attr(out, "is_satisfied")) {
  response_time <- c(response_time, rgamma(1, shape = 6.25, scale = 80))
  out <- seq_aipe_cv(response_time, width = 0.15)
}
out
#> Sequential check (coefficient of variation)
#> 
#>   Current n       : 53
#>   Criterion n     : 53
#>   Target width    : 0.15
#>   Confidence level: 95%
#>   Coverage        : asymptotic; assess with sensitivity analysis
#> 
#>   lower_limit       : 0.3167059
#>   cv                : 0.3814155
#>   upper_limit       : 0.4461252
#>   xi_squared        : 0.05777204
#>   criterion_n       : 53
#>   current_n         : 53
#> 
#>   Stopping rule met: TRUE
